topics.title: QS World University Rankings
bullets: The QS World University Rankings 2027 were released on 18 June 2026, assessing over 1,500 institutions across 106 countries and territories.
A record 52 Indian institutions have found a place in the rankings, making India the world's fifth most represented higher education system.
IIT Delhi emerged as India's highest-ranked institution for the second consecutive year, climbing to 118th position globally. What are the QS World University Rankings?
The QS World University Rankings are annual global university rankings published by Quacquarelli Symonds (QS), a British education organisation.
They are the second oldest global university rankings and one of the most widely referenced international league tables.
The rankings provide a comprehensive assessment of universities worldwide, helping students, academics, and policymakers compare institutions across multiple performance indicators.
QS was founded by Nunzio Quacquarelli in 1990 to provide information and advice to students looking to study abroad.
The first QS World University Rankings were released in October 2004 in partnership with Times Higher Education (THE).
In 2010, QS began publishing the rankings independently, using its own consistent and original methodology.
The first edition in 2004 featured just 200 institutions.
Today, the rankings evaluate over 1,500 institutions from an evaluated pool of 8,000+ universities worldwide.
The 2027 edition added 98 new institutions, with most entering in the 1,000–1,500 band.
The QS World University Rankings use a weighted framework combining reputation evidence, research performance, and employability outcomes.
The methodology is based on the aggregation of nine weighted indicators, each contributing a percentage to an institution’s final score.
The rankings draw on data from over 130,000 academics and 75,000+ employers worldwide.
Academic Reputation is the most heavily weighted indicator at 30%, reflecting the views of academics worldwide.
Citations per Faculty at 20% measures the research impact of an institution.
Employer Reputation at 15% reflects the views of employers on the quality of graduates. Recent Rankings –
The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) has retained the world's No. 1 position for the 15th consecutive year.
MIT's continued dominance underscores its exceptional research output, academic reputation, and innovation ecosystem.
The US continues to lead with 184 entries in the rankings, the highest of any country.
Imperial College London (UK) and Stanford University (US) are tied for second place in the 2027 rankings.
Imperial College London has maintained a place in the global top two for the third straight year.
Both institutions excelled across research impact, employer reputation, and academic reputation.
The University of Oxford (UK) ranks fourth in the QS World University Rankings 2027.
The university has consistently remained in the top five of the QS rankings for many years.
Harvard University (US) ranks fifth globally.
The US has 184 entries, followed by the UK (93) and mainland China (85).
The 2027 edition added 98 new institutions, most of them in the 1,000–1,500 band.
Central European University was the highest new entrant at 239th. India's Performance –
A record 52 Indian institutions have featured in the QS World University Rankings 2027.
This is up from just 14 a decade ago, reflecting India's growing influence in global higher education.
India is now the world's fifth most represented higher education system, behind the US, UK, mainland China, and Germany.
Among the 52 Indian institutions, 26 improved their positions, nine maintained their rankings, and 15 witnessed a decline.
Two Indian institutions entered the rankings for the first time - IIT (ISM) Dhanbad and Shoolini University.
The improvement reflects the impact of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and increased focus on research and internationalisation.
IIT Delhi has retained its position as India's highest-ranked university, climbing to 118th globally.
This marks a rise of five places from its previous rank of 123rd in 2026.
It equals the highest position ever achieved by an Indian institution in the QS World University Rankings.
IIT Delhi received an overall score of 65.7 points.
The institute performed exceptionally well in research impact, scoring an impressive 97.3 citations per faculty.
It improved in research, employability, and employer reputation, matching India's best-ever QS ranking.
IIT Bombay ranks 134th globally, slipping five places from its 2026 rank of 129.
Despite the slip, IIT Bombay remains one of India's top institutions, with a strong reputation in engineering and technology.
Its overall score was 63.9 points.
IIT Madras ranks 170th globally, making it the third Indian institution in the top 200.
IIT Madras has consistently performed well in research output and academic reputation.
Its overall score was 59.3 points.
IIT Kharagpur ranks 205th globally, maintaining its position among India's top institutions.
As India's oldest IIT, it has a strong legacy in engineering education and research.
Its overall score was 55.1 points.
The University of Delhi ranks 322nd globally, making it the top non-IIT institution in India.
It is one of India's largest and most prestigious universities, with a strong reputation in humanities, social sciences, and sciences.
Its overall score was 43.8 points.
IIT Delhi has improved its global ranking by 79 positions over the last four years, moving from 197th in 2024 to 118th in 2027.
This consistent upward trajectory reflects the institute's focus on research excellence, faculty quality, and international collaboration.
The improvement also highlights the growing global recognition of Indian higher education.
The number of Indian universities in the QS rankings has grown from 14 a decade ago to 52 in 2027.
India now has the fifth most represented higher education system in the world.
This expansion reflects India's increasing investment in higher education and the impact of reforms like the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020.

topics.title: G7 Meet
bullets: The 52nd G7 Summit was held from 15-17 June 2026 in Évian- les-Bains, France, under the French presidency.
The theme of the summit was "Forging New Partnerships and Rebuilding International Solidarity," reflecting the need for greater cooperation amid global challenges.
Leaders discussed economic resilience, AI governance, climate action, geopolitical conflicts. What is the G7? –
The G7 is an informal group of the world's leading advanced economies that meets annually to coordinate responses to major global challenges.
It is not a treaty-based institution and has no permanent secretariat, constitution, or headquarters.
The G7 operates through informal consultations and consensus- based decision-making, making it a powerful platform for international cooperation.
The Group was established as a platform for economic and financial cooperation in response to the 1973 energy crisis.
The G7 originated from a 1973 meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors in Paris, France.

This meeting was convened in response to major economic challenges of at time – an oil crisis, rising inflation and collapse of the Bretton Woods system. Under this, the value of the US dollar was fixed against gold.
In turn, other global currencies pegged their values to the dollar. But over time, the dollar was seen to have been overvalued against the fixed rate.
Therefore, a new mechanism had to be devised for exchange rates and this required global cooperation.
Thus, the idea of a forum was born, where major industrialised democracies could coordinate economic policies to address common challenges.
The G7 currently consists of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States.
The European Union also participates as a non-enumerated member.
Although G7 countries represent only about 10% of the world's population, they account for approximately 43% of global nominal GDP.
The G7 was established in 1975 as the G6 during the global economic crisis, with founding members France, West Germany, Italy, Japan, the UK, and the US.
In 1976, Canada joined, transforming it into the Group of Seven (G7).
Russia joined in 1998 (forming the G8) but was suspended in 2014 following its annexation of Crimea, returning the forum to the G7 format.
The first Summit of Heads of State and Government was held in 1975 in Rambouillet, France which included France, the United States of America, the United Kingdom, Germany, Japan, and Italy.
Since 1977, representatives of the European Economic Community, now the European Union, also participate in the work of the Group.
The EU does not hold the rotating presidency of the G7.
The presidency rotates annually among member countries; the host nation sets the summit agenda and organizes the meetings.
Throughout the year, ministerial meetings are held on finance, foreign affairs, climate, health, and other key sectors to prepare for the leaders' summit.
While it lacks a permanent administrative structure, the G7 rotates its presidency annually and the presidency serves as a temporary secretariat.
However, its relevance has been questioned in recent years as the combined share of its members in global GDP has fallen.
An analysis from the think tank Bruegel (‘The G7 is dead, long live the G7’) said it declined from roughly 50% in the 1970s to around 30% in 2018.
In comparison, the G20, which was established in response to the 2008 financial crisis, is seen as a more inclusive forum. 2026 Meet –
The summit was held at the lakeside resort of Évian-les-Bains in the French Alps, from 15 to 17 June 2026.
The location was chosen for its scenic setting and to facilitate informal discussions among world leaders.
Évian-les-Bains has previously hosted international summits, providing a neutral and conducive environment for diplomacy.
The theme, "Forging New Partnerships and Rebuilding International Solidarity," emphasized the need for unity in a fragmented world.
France set three key priorities: Artificial Intelligence (AI) governance, economic resilience, and international security.
India was invited as a special guest to represent the concerns of the Global South.
France invited over 10 countries and international organizations to the Outreach Sessions.
Guest countries included India, Brazil, South Korea, Kenya, Egypt, Ukraine, the UAE, and Qatar. Day 1 Highlights –
The summit opened with leaders focusing on the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the West Asia crisis.
Leaders reaffirmed their support for Ukraine, pledging additional air defence systems, interceptors, and long-range ammunition.
Discussions also centered on energy security and the impact of disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
G7 leaders welcomed the US-Iran deal to end the West Asia war, calling it a "historic opportunity".
The leaders expressed readiness to contribute to its implementation, including efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
US President Donald Trump emphasized that the agreement was a memorandum of understanding and that he was ready to resume military action if Iran did not comply.
The summit was held amid protests and heightened security concerns.
French authorities faced challenges including network attacks, potential sabotage, and cross-border coordination issues.
Despite the protests, the summit proceeded with its scheduled agenda.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressed the Outreach Session, stating that the world suffers from a shortage of trust.
He emphasized that many global crises stem from a lack of trust rather than a shortage of resources.
Modi called for strengthening confidence among nations to address economic, security, and developmental challenges. Day 2 Highlights –
Day 2 featured a dedicated session on Artificial Intelligence, with leaders discussing its risks and opportunities.

For the first time in G7 history, CEOs of leading AI companies – including Sam Altman (OpenAI), Demis Hassabis (Google DeepMind), and Dario Amodei (Anthropic) – were invited to the decision-making table.
OpenAI chief Sam Altman urged governments "not to cede responsibilities to AI labs" and to set global standards for AI deployment.
G7 leaders pledged closer coordination on the risks and opportunities of advanced AI.
They discussed creating a "trusted partners" scheme granting non-US nations access to advanced US AI models from firms like Anthropic.
Leaders also called on tech firms to build tools ensuring minors stay safe online amid AI concerns.
G7 leaders agreed to "significantly" reduce dependency on China as a supplier of critical minerals.
The target is to reduce dependency to under 60% by 2030, with an ambition to reach 50% as soon as possible.
Leaders reaffirmed the urgency of diversifying supply chains and building collective resilience.
Prime Minister Modi warned against the misuse of AI, stating that without safeguards, it could expose children to risks of misinformation, deepfakes, and exploitation.
He called for strengthening global cooperation against deepfakes, misinformation, and cyber fraud.
Modi highlighted that AI can educate children in their own languages and personalise learning, but safeguards are essential.
Modi pitched for setting up a global framework to boost cooperation on connectivity and trade – the International Mobilisation Partnership for Accelerating Connectivity and Trade (IMPACT).
He proposed that the framework be modelled on the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC).
The idea is to combine G7 capital, India's talent, and the ownership of Global South countries. Day 3 Highlights –
On the final day, Donald Trump strode into the morning session and declared "I'm the boss," drawing laughter from other leaders including host Emmanuel Macron.
The moment highlighted the assertive US presence at the summit and Trump's personal style of diplomacy.
Despite the light-hearted moment, serious discussions continued on AI, economic growth, and global security.
G7 leaders reaffirmed their unity in support of Ukraine, including its territorial integrity.
They agreed to increase pressure on the Russian war economy, including strengthening sanctions on the oil and gas sectors.
Leaders also pledged to diversify energy supply routes and reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz.
The summit concluded without a final communique, marking the second consecutive year without a joint statement.
Instead, nine separate deliverables were published, covering geopolitics, the global economy, and public health.
This reflects the challenges of achieving consensus among the G7 on contentious issues.
G7 leaders reaffirmed their commitment to existing G7 exchange rate commitments amid financial market turbulence.
They encouraged oil-importing countries to establish sufficient oil reserve systems aligned with the IEA 90-day stockpiling requirement.
Leaders also committed to strengthening investigations to freeze and seize assets, including virtual assets, to target organised crime networks. PM Modi's Bilateral Meetings –
Prime Minister Narendra Modi held a series of high-level bilateral meetings on the sidelines of the G7 Summit.
These meetings focused on boosting trade, investment, and strategic partnerships across various sectors.
Modi used the platform to amplify the voice of the Global South and advocate for inclusive global governance.
Modi met Trump for the first time in 16 months, marking a reset in bilateral ties after a period of strain.
Modi and UK PM Keir Starmer announced that the India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) will enter into force on 15 July 2026.
The agreement is expected to significantly boost bilateral trade and investment and make it easier for Indian professionals to work in the UK.
Modi met with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa.
They announced that the India-EU Free Trade Agreement will be signed by the end of 2026.
The negotiations concluded during the 16th India-EU Summit in New Delhi on 27 January 2026.

List of leaders Prime Minister Narendra Modi met on the sidelines of the G7 Summit 2026 in Évian-les-Bains, France: 1. French President Emmanuel Macron, 2. US President Donald Trump, 3. UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer, 4. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, 5. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, 6. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, 7. UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, 8. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, 9. South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, 10.Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, 11.Kenyan President William Ruto, 12.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, 13.European Council President António Costa, and 14.Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
The 53rd G7 Summit will be hosted by Germany, as the presidency rotates annually among member countries.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will chair the summit, which is expected to build on the discussions held in Évian.

The venue and exact dates for the 2027 summit are yet to be announced. Passage: The 2026 G7 Summit brought together leaders of major advanced economies to discuss global security, economic stability, artificial intelligence governance, energy security, critical mineral supply chains, and ongoing geopolitical conflicts. The summit took place amid continuing concerns regarding the wars in Ukraine and West Asia, as well as debates over climate finance and reform of international institutions. The G7 remains an influential informal grouping despite the growing economic weight of emerging economies. Outreach countries, including India, participated in discussions on issues requiring wider international cooperation. The summit also highlighted efforts to reduce strategic dependence on vulnerable supply chains and strengthen cooperation in emerging technologies. Source: Times of India
